subject: Business Models
title: MoviePass: Unlimited Movies, No Math
description: A quick win: understand MoviePass: Unlimited Movies, No Math.

hook.text: MoviePass offered unlimited movie tickets for $10/month. A single ticket costs $15. The math was obvious.

buildup.text: MoviePass bet that most subscribers wouldn't go frequently. Heavy users would be subsidized by light ones.

discovery.text: The opposite happened. MoviePass attracted movie fans who went 3-5 times a month. It lost $20+ per active user monthly.

twist.text: MoviePass secretly limited showtimes and blocked popular films to reduce losses. Users felt deceived and canceled.

climax.text: MoviePass went from 3 million subscribers to shutdown. Unsustainable pricing attracts the worst-case customer.

punchline.text: $10/month, $15 tickets. The customers who signed up would bankrupt you.

quiz.question: What phenomenon doomed MoviePass?
options: Heavy users who went 3-5 times monthly were attracted by the pricing

details.summary: MoviePass offered unlimited movie theater tickets for 9.95 dollars per month, far below the cost of a single ticket. It attracted 3 million subscribers but was paying full price to theaters for each visit, losing money on virtually every customer every month.
details.whyItMatters: MoviePass is a textbook case of subsidizing demand without a path to profitability. The hope that data monetization or theater partnerships would eventually cover losses proved completely wrong, burning through hundreds of millions in cash.
takeaways: Unlimited movies at 9.95 dollars per month lost money on nearly every subscriber
Three million subscribers generated massive losses with no revenue offset
Data monetization and theater partnerships never materialized as hoped

faq.question: How much money did MoviePass lose per subscriber?
faq.answer: Active subscribers averaged 1.5 movie visits per month at an average ticket price of 11 dollars. MoviePass paid theaters full price for each ticket but charged subscribers only 9.95 per month. That means roughly 6 to 7 dollars lost per active subscriber per month.

faq.question: Could a movie subscription model ever work profitably?
faq.answer: AMC's A-List charges 22 to 25 dollars monthly for three movies per week at its own theaters, controlling both the subscription and venue costs. Keeping customers in-house for concession sales adds revenue. Ownership of theaters is the key difference from MoviePass.
